questions.question: What are the differences between Docker bridge, host, and overlay networking modes?
questions.title: Docker Networking: Bridge vs Host vs Overlay
questions.direct_answer: Bridge network (default) creates an isolated virtual network per host; containers communicate via container names. Host network removes network isolation — container shares the host network stack directly. Overlay network spans multiple Docker hosts (Swarm/Kubernetes) enabling cross-node container communication. Most Spring Boot apps use bridge locally and overlay (via CNI) in Kubernetes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Docker networking knowledge and understanding of when each mode is appropriate

sections.title: The Port-Mapping Mistake That Reveals a Networking Misunderstanding
sections.content:
The most common Docker networking error in Spring Boot projects is adding `-p 5432:5432` so the app container can talk to the PostgreSQL container — then wondering why the connection uses `localhost`. Containers on the same Docker network reach each other by **service name**, not by published ports. Publishing a port exposes it to the host machine and the outside world, which is exactly what you do not want for internal database traffic.

This misunderstanding stems from conflating two different communication paths: **east-west traffic** (container to container on the same network) and **north-south traffic** (external client to container). Bridge networking handles east-west traffic through Docker's built-in DNS resolver. Host networking removes the network boundary entirely. Overlay networking extends east-west communication across multiple physical machines.

Each mode solves a different problem, and choosing the wrong one creates either unnecessary exposure, performance overhead, or communication failures. The decision framework is straightforward once you understand what each mode actually does to the network stack.

sections.title: Bridge vs Host vs Overlay — What Each Mode Actually Changes
sections.content:
The three modes differ in isolation, DNS behavior, and scope. Understanding these differences prevents the port-mapping mistake and clarifies when each mode is appropriate.

| Dimension | Bridge | Host | Overlay |
|---|---|---|---|
| Network isolation | Isolated virtual network per host | None — shares host network stack | Isolated virtual network across hosts |
| Container DNS | Service name resolves automatically | Uses host DNS, no container names | Service name resolves across nodes |
| Port mapping needed | Only for external access (`-p`) | Not needed — binds directly to host | Via ingress routing or service mesh |
| Performance | Good — minimal NAT overhead | Best — zero NAT, zero bridge | VXLAN encapsulation adds ~5% overhead |
| Multi-host support | Single host only | Single host only | Spans multiple Docker hosts |
| Security surface | Containers isolated from host | Container ports exposed on host directly | Encrypted tunnels between nodes |
| Kubernetes equivalent | Pod-internal network | `hostNetwork: true` | CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Cilium) |

Docker Compose automatically creates a **user-defined bridge network** for each project. Every service in the compose file joins this network and can reach every other service by its service name. This is why `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/myapp` works without any port configuration — Docker's embedded DNS resolves `postgres` to the container's internal IP.

sections.title: Matching the Network Mode to Your Deployment Model
sections.content:
For **local development** with Docker Compose, the default bridge network handles everything. Your Spring Boot app connects to PostgreSQL using the service name `postgres`, and Redis using `redis`. Port mappings with `-p` should only appear when you need host access — for example, exposing `5432` so DBeaver on your laptop can query the database directly.

A common compose setup illustrates this — the app reaches postgres by service name without any published ports between containers, and only the app port is exposed to the host.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    # No ports needed for app-to-postgres communication
```

**Host networking** removes all isolation — the container's processes bind directly to the host's network interfaces. The performance benefit is measurable for high-throughput workloads like Kafka brokers or network monitoring tools where even bridge NAT overhead matters. But it sacrifices isolation and risks port conflicts with host services, so use it only when benchmarks justify it.

**Overlay networking** spans multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN tunneling and is the foundation of Docker Swarm's multi-node communication. In practice, if you deploy on Kubernetes — which most production Java teams do — the CNI plugin handles overlay networking transparently. You configure Services and NetworkPolicies rather than managing overlay networks directly. Understanding overlay concepts still matters because the same DNS resolution and network segmentation principles apply in both Swarm and Kubernetes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Service names are DNS entries on bridge networks** — Docker Compose containers reach each other at `postgres:5432` or `redis:6379` without port mapping, because Docker's embedded DNS resolves service names to container IPs
- **Port mapping (`-p`) is for north-south traffic only** — publishing ports exposes them to the host and external clients; container-to-container communication never needs it and adding it creates unnecessary attack surface
- **Host networking removes all isolation for zero NAT** — the container binds directly to host interfaces, giving best performance but risking port collisions and eliminating network-level security boundaries
- **Overlay uses VXLAN tunneling across hosts** — adds roughly 5% overhead from encapsulation but enables cross-node communication in Docker Swarm; Kubernetes CNI plugins provide the production equivalent
- **User-defined bridge networks outperform the default bridge** — the default `bridge` network lacks automatic DNS resolution; docker-compose creates user-defined networks with DNS built in, which is why service-name connectivity works out of the box

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker provides three main network drivers, and choosing the wrong one is the most common reason containers cannot communicate or performance is unexpectedly poor.

**Bridge — the default for single-host communication**
- Every Docker installation creates a default `bridge` network; containers on the same bridge can reach each other by IP, but not by name — user-defined bridge networks enable DNS-based service discovery, which is why you should always create a named bridge and never rely on the default
- Create a user-defined bridge with `docker network create app-network`; containers on it resolve each other by container name — `http://postgres:5432` works from a Spring Boot container if both containers join the same named bridge
- The default bridge network requires you to use `--link` (deprecated) for name resolution, which is why Docker Compose creates a project-specific network by default

**Host — for performance-sensitive workloads**
- `--network host` removes the network namespace boundary; the container uses the host's network stack directly — no NAT, no port mapping overhead, but the container shares the host's IP and port space
- A container on host networking binds ports directly on the host; two containers cannot both bind port 8080 on the same host network
- Appropriate for high-throughput, latency-sensitive workloads where NAT overhead is measurable — avoid it for most application containers because it reduces isolation

**Overlay — for multi-host communication**
- Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN encapsulation; they are the foundation of Docker Swarm and Kubernetes pod networking
- Services on a Swarm overlay network communicate using the service name as hostname across any node in the cluster — the routing mesh handles which container on which host receives the request
- A misconfigured overlay is usually a firewall rule issue: UDP port 4789 (VXLAN) and TCP port 7946 (control plane) must be open between all nodes
